questions.q: « Je vais à Paris. » → « J'___ vais. »
questions.why: Y replaces a place, whatever the preposition: à, en, dans, sur, chez. En would mean coming back from there.

questions.q: « Je parle de mon travail. » → « J'___ parle. »
questions.why: En replaces de + something. The verb decides: parler de gives en, penser à gives y.

questions.q: Complete: « J'ai besoin d'aide. » → « J'___ ai besoin. »
questions.why: Avoir besoin de contains de, so the replacement is en. Every avoir + noun expression behaves this way.

questions.q: Complete: « Je pense à mon travail. » → « J'___ pense. »
questions.why: Penser à a thing gives y. If it were a person you could not use y: je pense à lui.

questions.q: « Je pense à mon frère. » → how do you replace « à mon frère » ?
questions.why: Y is for things and places only. With penser à and s'intéresser à, a person is picked up by a stressed pronoun kept after the verb.

questions.q: « Tu veux du café ? » — how do you say « Yes, I do » in French?
questions.why: English can drop some; French cannot drop en. Whenever the noun disappears but a quantity is implied, en has to appear.

questions.q: Complete: « J'ai deux frères. » → « J'en ai ___. »
questions.why: The number stays, at the end: subject + en + verb + amount. En on its own would not say how many.

questions.q: « J'ai un frère. » → which is right?
questions.why: Un and une survive as numbers at the end, exactly like deux or trois. Dropping it leaves the sentence incomplete.
Y then en, always in that order and always last in the queue. This is the phrase to anchor the whole order table.

questions.q: Build the sentence: He gives it to me.
questions.why: Column 1 (me, te, se, nous, vous) comes before column 2 (le, la, les). Il le me donne is not possible.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I give it to him.
questions.why: Here it is column 2 before column 3: le, la, les come before lui and leur. Note the order flips compared with me le donne.

questions.q: Put the pronouns in: « (te, en) Je ___ parle. »
questions.why: Te is column 1 and en is always last, so t'en. Te elides to t' before the vowel of en.

questions.q: Which is the correct positive command for « Give it to me » ?
questions.why: After a positive imperative the pronouns follow the verb and the direct object comes first, with me becoming moi. The negative reverts: ne me le donne pas.
Give me some. Even after the verb, en stays last, and moi shrinks back to m' before it.

questions.q: State when you use y, when en, and when neither will do. Give an example of each.
a: Y replaces à or any preposition of place plus a thing: j'y vais, j'y pense, il y répond. En replaces de plus something, and any quantity: j'en parle, j'en ai besoin, j'en veux, j'en ai deux. Neither works for a person: à + person is lui / leur (je lui parle) or a stressed pronoun with penser à (je pense à lui), and de + person is de + stressed pronoun (je parle d'elle). Order: y and en come last, in that order — il y en a.
questions.why: The split is thing or place versus person, then à versus de. Getting it wrong is one of the most audible learner mistakes.
